extracted.intended_audience: Title IX coordinators, investigators, decision-makers, institutional administrators, and legal counsel at educational institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory requirements for how educational institutions must conduct Title IX grievance processes for sexual harassment allegations, including investigation, evidence, dismissal, consolidation, training, confidentiality, and appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretionary dismissal grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(3)(ii) permits (but does not require) a recipient to dismiss a formal complaint (or allegations therein) in three situations: where a complainant notifies the Title IX Coordinator in writing that the complainant wishes to withdraw the formal complaint or any allegations; where the respondent is no longer enrolled or employed by the recipient; or where specific circumstances prevent the recipient from gathering evidence sufficient to reach a determination as to the allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This discretionary dismissal is not equivalent to concluding that the evidence fails to meet a burden of proof or is meritless; it should be applied narrowly where specific circumstances prevent the recipient from meeting its burden to gather sufficient evidence. A recipient should not apply discretionary dismissal simply because it is uncertain whether it can meet its burden of proof. The provision preserves recipient discretion to account for unique facts and circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written notice and appeal of dismissal decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(3)(iii) requires the recipient to promptly send the parties written notice when a formal complaint (or allegations therein) has been dismissed (mandatory or discretionary), including the reason for the dismissal; §106.45(b)(8) is revised to allow both parties equal opportunity to appeal any dismissal decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt written notice promotes clarity and transparency so parties know when and why a matter has been dismissed. Parties have equal appellate rights to challenge dismissal decisions; appealable bases include newly discovered evidence, procedural irregularity, or bias/conflict of interest (see appeals metric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation of formal complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(4) gives recipients discretion to consolidate formal complaints of sexual harassment when the allegations arise out of the same facts or circumstances, including situations with more than one complainant or respondent and counter-complaints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where consolidation occurs, singular references to 'party', 'complainant', or 'respondent' in §106.45 include the plural. Consolidation is discretionary and intended to provide clarity for incidents involving multiple parties or interrelated allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient's burden to gather evidence and present to decision-maker
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(5)(i) places the burdens of gathering evidence (and presenting evidence for the decision-maker to evaluate under the recipient's chosen standard of evidence) on the recipient, not on the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must undertake a thorough search for relevant facts and evidence, but within constraints such as reasonably prompt timeframes and without subpoena power. The recipient must act impartially and objectively; bearing the burden does not make the recipient a 'prosecutor' but requires it to gather and present both inculpatory and exculpatory evidence to enable a fair determination. The Department declined to limit the burden to only 'reasonably available' evidence or to require pursuing 'all' leads, balancing thoroughness with practical constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal opportunity to present witnesses and evidence (including experts)
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(5)(ii) requires recipients to provide equal opportunity for all parties to present both fact and expert witnesses and to present inculpatory and exculpatory evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision is intended to improve fairness, reliability, and legitimacy of outcomes. Recipients must allow parties to participate fully in investigation and adjudication by gathering evidence, presenting witnesses, reviewing evidence, and responding to investigative reports. The Department acknowledged concerns about intimidation/retaliation and addressed them via anti-retaliation/confidentiality rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to inspect and review evidence; live hearing questioning
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(5)(vi) gives both parties equal opportunity to inspect and review all evidence directly related to the allegations. §§106.45(b)(6)(i)-(ii) direct decision-makers to allow parties to ask all relevant questions and follow-up questions at a live hearing, with only relevant cross-examination questions permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties must be given meaningful opportunities to see and respond to the evidence that will be considered. Training and rules should clarify what questions are 'relevant' and what cross-examination is permitted; party witnesses must be subject to permitted cross-examination to have their statements considered in certain postsecondary adjudications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence deemed not relevant or barred from use
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45 specifies categories of information that are not relevant or are barred from use in a grievance process: information protected by a legally recognized privilege; evidence about a complainant's prior sexual history; any party's medical, psychological, and similar treatment records unless the party has given voluntary, written consent; and (for postsecondary adjudications) party or witness statements not subjected to cross-examination at a live hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may not adopt evidentiary rules that contravene these exclusions. For example, a recipient may not exclude evidence solely because its probative value is substantially outweighed by danger of unfair prejudice (the Federal Rules balancing test) if that exclusion conflicts with §106.45. The regulations focus investigation and adjudication on evidence material to proving the allegations while protecting privacy and privileged information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients' discretion on evidentiary evaluation but equal application required
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients have discretion to adopt rules regarding how admissible, relevant evidence is evaluated for weight or credibility, provided such rules do not conflict with §106.45 and apply equally to both parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may adopt rules (for example, about assigning weight to evidence of prior bad acts) so long as the rules are neutrally applied to complainants and respondents alike. Any such rules should be reflected in the training materials for Title IX personnel and made publicly available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-restriction on parties discussing allegations and gathering evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(5)(iii) requires that recipients must not restrict either party's ability to (i) discuss the allegations under investigation or (ii) gather and present relevant evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prohibits prior restraints or 'gag orders' that prevent parties from speaking with parents, friends, advocates, or potential witnesses, though commenters raised concerns about privacy, retaliation, witness tampering, and stigma. The provision distinguishes between a party's speech and the recipient's obligation to conduct an objective investigation; recipients retain ability to adopt neutral rules about conduct (e.g., no-contact orders) so long as rules are applied equally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-retaliation and confidentiality protections
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.71 expressly prohibits any person from intimidating, threatening, coercing, or discriminating against another individual for the purpose of interfering with any right or privilege secured by Title IX, and requires that identities of complainants, respondents, and witnesses be kept confidential except as permitted by FERPA, required by law, or to the extent necessary to carry out a Title IX grievance process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These protections are intended to deter retaliation, enable parties to discuss allegations and gather evidence without fear, and provide mechanisms to file retaliation complaints under §106.8(c). Confidentiality has statutory exceptions when necessary to conduct the grievance process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training requirements and public availability of training materials
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(1)(iii) requires investigators and decision-makers to receive training on issues of relevance (including when questions about a complainant's prior sexual history are not relevant) and on how to conduct investigations and grievance processes. §106.45(b)(10) requires recipients to make training materials publicly available on their websites or available upon request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training must cover the recipient's procedural and evidentiary rules, issues of relevance, and any instructions about evaluating or assigning weight to types of evidence. Public availability of training materials improves transparency and helps parties and the public understand the grievance process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals: permissible bases and equal opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations revise appeals provisions to allow both parties equal opportunity to appeal dismissal decisions and other outcomes on specified bases, including newly discovered evidence that may affect the outcome, procedural irregularity, or conflict of interest/bias that may have affected the outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals provide a mechanism to correct errors such as an inappropriate dismissal (e.g., where newly discovered evidence shows conduct meets the definition of sexual harassment) or procedural irregularities. Recipients must afford equal appellate opportunities to both complainants and respondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on scope of investigation and reasonableness standard
rubrics_metrics.description: While recipients are obligated to undertake a thorough search for relevant facts and evidence, the Department recognizes limitations: investigations must be conducted and concluded within designated, reasonably prompt time frames and recipients lack subpoena power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulations strike a balance between expecting recipients to gather evidence 'available' to them and not imposing impractical obligations (such as compulsory pursuit of all leads). Recipients are expected to be thorough but reasonable given timeframes and authority constraints; commenters' suggestions to narrow or broaden this obligation were declined in favor of the balanced approach.
